extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims integrate judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) into a practical application under the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B). Focuses on identifying mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, and field-of-use limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that amount to nothing more than an instruction to apply the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) are not patent-eligible. For example, claims that amount to nothing more than an instruction to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the abstract idea eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court cases (Alice, Mayo, Gottschalk v. Benson) show that reciting a judicial exception plus generic application (e.g., 'apply it' on a generic computer) is insufficient. Examiners should explain why recited elements do not meaningfully limit the claim when claiming implementation on a generic computer. Consider overlap with other considerations (improvement to computer or technology, particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional) to determine whether elements are more than mere instructions to apply an exception. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Recitation of claim limitations that attempt to cover any solution with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented or functional claiming that covers any solution to an identified problem is equivalent to the words 'apply it' and has been found ineligible (Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents v. Active Network). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or way to achieve an outcome may integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. Use case examples (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One; Electric Power) to explain why additional limitations are merely result-oriented or instead supply meaningful technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process. Use of a computer or other machinery in its ordinary capacity (to receive, store, transmit data, etc.) or simply adding a general-purpose computer to an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto; Alice; Gottschalk v. Benson; Versata; FairWarning) show invoking generic devices in their ordinary capacity is insufficient. Conversely, claims that improve computer capabilities or an existing technology (e.g., McRO, Enfish) may integrate the exception. Examiners should identify whether the claimed machine elements merely perform conventional tasks or instead provide technical improvements to the machine/technology (see MPEP §§2106.04(d)(1), 2106.05(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the application of the judicial exception is particular and confined to a practical application or is overly general and broad across many fields. Broad applicability across many fields may not provide meaningful limitations and may amount to merely adding the words 'apply it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that generically recites an effect or claims every mode of accomplishing the effect describes the result or effect dissociated from any method and does not meaningfully limit the claim (Internet Patents v. Active Network; O’Reilly v. Morse; The Telephone Cases). Limitations that confine the exception to a particular practical application (see BASCOM, DDR Holdings, Thales Visionix) may amount to significantly more if they recite technical means or manipulations of the environment that provide a technological solution to a technological problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements add more than insignificant 'extra-solution activity' to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' are activities incidental to the primary process/product that are merely nominal or tangential additions to the claim (includes pre-solution and post-solution activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pre-solution data gathering (obtaining information), post-solution outputting (printing a report). Supreme Court (Flook, Mayo) held that adding insignificant post-solution or conventional activity does not amount to an inventive concept. Evaluate this consideration in Step 2A Prong Two (and note overlap with Step 2B well-understood/routine/conventional). Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its merits and may rely on other considerations (particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, field-of-use) to decide whether extra-solution activity is insignificant. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for rejection drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known (i.e., token or conventional activity). Well-known activities used in conjunction with a judicial exception are token extra-solution activity and should not be considered in the Step 2A Prong Two extra-solution activity analysis because this overlaps with the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration evaluated in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Bilski (well-known random analysis techniques), Flook (use with existing surveying techniques), Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem. (use of well-known XML tag). Because this consideration overlaps with conventionality, do not re-evaluate it in Step 2A Prong Two; reserve conventionality analysis for Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation is significant (imposes meaningful limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim so that it is not nominally or tangentially related to the invention. If the limitation is insignificant or merely restricts public access, it may be token extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where courts found limitations insignificant: Ultramercial (restricting public access to media), Apple v. Ameranth (menu ordering features), Ultramercial/In re Brown examples. This consideration applies in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should explain why a limitation is or is not meaningful in the context of claim as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting (i.e., all uses of the recited judicial exception require such data gathering or output). If so, the limitation may be mere data gathering/insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Mayo (measuring metabolites), OIP Technologies v. Amazon (presenting offers and gathering statistics), CyberSource v. Retail Decisions (verifying credit-card transactions). Data collection, testing, logging, presenting offers, obtaining transaction info have been treated as mere data gathering. Use these precedents to assess whether claimed data-related steps meaningfully limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of activities found to be insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of activities have been treated as insignificant extra-solution activity by the courts, including mere data gathering, selecting a particular data source or type, and insignificant applications (conventional post-solution actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere data gathering examples: performing clinical tests to obtain inputs (In re Grams), system testing for responses (In re Meyers), presenting offers and gathering statistics (OIP Technologies), consulting/updating logs (Ultramercial), determining biomarker levels (Mayo). Selecting particular data sources/types examples: limiting a database index to XML tags (Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem.), taking orders from a subset of customers (Ameranth), selecting power-grid data (Electric Power Group). Insignificant application examples: cutting hair after selecting style (In re Brown), printing/downloading menus (Ameranth). Examiners should cite and explain when relying on such analogies in rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use and technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements amount to more than generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply the exception does not add significantly more and cannot integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parker v. Flook is a classic example where limiting an abstract idea to a field of use was insufficient. Diamond v. Diehr illustrates contrast where specific, concerted steps transformed raw material and were sufficient. Affinity Labs v. DirecTV shows that limiting an abstract idea to a particular device (cellular telephone) was not enough. Examples of field-of-use limitations deemed token include limiting drug administration to a patient population (Mayo), identifying financial-market participants (Bilski), limiting a formula to wheel circumference (Flook), and limiting collection/analysis to power-grid data (Electric Power). Examiners should treat technological environment/field-of-use limitations as interchangeable and consider overlap with extra-solution activity and other considerations when forming rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must explain why additional elements do not meaningfully limit the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that do not amount to more than a recitation of 'apply it' (or equivalent), examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific reasoning in the rejection (e.g., implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer does not integrate it into a practical application in Step 2A Prong Two or add significantly more in Step 2B). Cite relevant case law (Alice, Mayo) and MPEP §2106.07(a) for guidance on drafting subject matter eligibility rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not evaluate well-understood, routine, conventional in Step 2A Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural requirement: the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration is only evaluated in Step 2B and should not be evaluated in Step 2A Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance notes repeated admonitions that certain considerations overlap (e.g., extra-solution activity vs. conventionality) but instruct examiners to reserve the well-understood, routine, conventional analysis for Step 2B to avoid double-counting. Use other considerations (particular machine/transformation, field-of-use) in Step 2A Prong Two and rely on Step 2B for conventionality analysis.
